title: Policy Is Not Permission: How Executives Make AI Governance Work
subtitle: Six proofs before AI can act: a business-first approach to visibility, bounded authority, runtime controls, accountability and cost.
content_html:
The Leadership Decision: What must a business know before allowing AI to act, and what would justify keeping that permission? I would start with a named process owner, an explicitly limited action and a control the business can demonstrate at the moment of execution. An approved policy, a compliant supplier or a successful pilot may support the case. None proves that the system will refuse an action outside its authority.

Next move: Select three AI-enabled workflows with consequences for customers, records, access or cost. Ask the owners to show one permitted action, one prohibited action, the actual enforcement point and the evidence supporting both outcomes. That demonstration will reveal more than another inventory presentation.

The six operating proofs

Many organisations already have policies, legal reviews, architecture standards and control libraries. The gap is often between those documents and what a system is allowed to do during a real transaction. The six proofs below connect the business purpose to a continuing permission, without demanding the same bureaucracy for every use case.

  1. Business case. Which outcome is the AI expected to improve, and who owns it? Show expected value after licence, supervision, exception handling and recovery costs. A faster AI task is not a business benefit if its unfinished work moves elsewhere.
  2. Complete discovery. Which workflows use AI, including features added to applications purchased before AI became commonplace? Include internal agents, embedded models, connected tools, suppliers, data access and the actions they can actually trigger. A software inventory alone will miss some consequential uses.
  3. Rules and risk. Which laws apply to this activity, location, provider or deployer, data and affected people? Map required duties, relevant standards, security threats and business impact to testable conditions. Assess not only whether an action can be reversed, but what correction would cost and what harm may occur before reversal.
  4. Bounded authority. Specify the approved identity, purpose, data, tool, action, monetary or transaction limit, expiry and human approval threshold. A grant at the beginning of a task should not be treated as unrestricted permission for later steps. Assign someone with authority to withdraw it.
  5. Enforcement at execution. Recheck permission immediately before the consequential action occurs, including scope and current identity. A policy written in a handbook or placed in a model prompt is not a substitute for a control in the execution path. Test that attempts to bypass approval, exceed a limit or use a compromised connector are denied or escalated.
  6. Operating evidence. Link the business decision and each material condition to a responsible person, enforced control, test, exception and review date. Monitor changes in suppliers, tools, permissions, incidents and actual process outcomes. Continued permission must be a decision supported by current evidence rather than an inherited project status.

Choose the autonomy the business can justify

There are three useful management choices: observe, where AI detects or summarises without changing the underlying process; recommend with review, where a person approves the proposed action; and act within limits, where AI executes a defined class of actions under enforced boundaries. These are operating choices, not legal risk categories or maturity stages. Higher autonomy should follow the consequence of failure, the ability to intervene and the quality of evidence, not simply confidence in a model demonstration.

A technically reversible action may still be expensive to undo. An incorrect customer commitment, account change or access grant can be corrected later but create immediate commercial, privacy or trust consequences. For lower-impact tasks, sampling and monitoring may be enough; a decision affecting rights, money or sensitive access may need action-specific approval or may not justify autonomous execution at all.

Illustrative composite, not a reported engagement: An AI service assistant reviews a case, drafts a response and proposes a record update. Drafting can be allowed under an approved data boundary, while sending a binding commitment needs a valid case-specific approval at execution. A change in the user's role or the recipient after the initial approval should cause a fresh check or a refusal. The governance design is only credible if the team can demonstrate both the approved path and a blocked attempt.

The executive decision record

For a material workflow, I would want a single record that a business owner and an independent reviewer can examine without reconstructing the project. The following is a hypothetical example of how an AI-assisted customer-service process could be presented at a steering committee:

  • Purpose and owner: Reduce time spent drafting routine replies; the service process owner remains accountable for customer outcomes.
  • Permitted scope: Classify a case and prepare a draft using approved information. No autonomous contractual commitments or access changes.
  • Approval boundary: A named, currently authorised reviewer must approve any binding communication for the exact case and recipient.
  • Enforcement proof: Execution-path tests show that expired authority, changed recipients and actions beyond the approved scope are blocked.
  • Exceptions and stop rule: An attempted bypass, material supplier change or unexplained sensitive-data exposure pauses the affected action until reviewed.
  • Renewal and value: Review after a defined operating period and any significant change, using error rates, overrides, recovery time, customer outcomes and net economic benefit.

The record joins legal and security requirements to the business consequence without turning the executive into a security engineer. It also makes escalation explicit: the process owner owns the outcome, security and privacy owners test their controls, and the designated authority decides whether the permission continues. An auditor can then trace an obligation through a working test to a recorded decision.

What governance costs—and what it is worth

Controls are not free. Stronger approval gates may reduce risk but increase waiting time, human review and the cost of operating a service. I would assess governance alongside the business case, not as a separate compliance overhead that becomes visible only after deployment.

Illustrative calculation, not observed performance: Suppose AI prepares drafts for 1,000 service cases per month, removing three minutes of drafting per case: 50 hours of gross time saved. If review takes one minute per case (about 16.7 hours), exceptions consume 12 hours and monitoring another six, the net capacity released is about 15.3 hours before software, infrastructure and recovery costs. The result may still justify the design if accuracy and customer outcomes improve; it may not if the workload or error cost is higher. Leaders should change the autonomy level or stop the use case when the evidence no longer supports the trade-off.

A practical scorecard would show the share of material workflows with current owners and authority records, the share of consequential actions that passed an independent deny-or-escalate test, outstanding exceptions and the benefit after the cost of control. Each percentage needs a denominator and review date. Counting completed checklists or active AI users cannot substitute for evidence from the process.

Use laws, standards and security references for their proper purpose

Law sets the applicable duties. The EU AI Act, GDPR and, where relevant, DORA and NIS2 address different legal concerns. Applicability depends on the business activity, geography, sector, affected people and the company's role. As of 7 November 2026, the amended EU AI Act has staggered provisions: many rules apply from 2 August 2026, while certain Annex III high-risk obligations apply from 2 December 2027 and Annex I product-related high-risk obligations from 2 August 2028. Regulatory specialists should verify scope and transitional conditions for the specific workflow; rules in other jurisdictions must be assessed separately.

Standards help organise management and assurance. ISO/IEC 42001:2023 concerns AI management systems, ISO/IEC 23894:2023 addresses AI risk and ISO/IEC 27090:2026 addresses AI-related cybersecurity threats. ISO/IEC 42007 is still in draft as of this review. NIST AI RMF and Singapore's agentic AI governance framework are useful voluntary guidance; they are not substitutes for law or proof that a particular deployment is compliant.

Security references help teams find the ways controls could fail. OWASP's LLM and Agentic Top 10, MITRE ATLAS, CSA MAESTRO and the CSA AI Controls Matrix can guide threat analysis and independent testing. Suitable technical controls may include scoped identity and expiring permissions, gateways, policy engines, tracing, data safeguards, red-team exercises, supplier review and a tested stop mechanism. Buy or build what closes an identified risk gap; a long catalogue is not evidence that the controls are working.

A first 90-day management sequence

During the first 30 days, identify and prioritise consequential workflows, including AI embedded in existing applications; establish owners, current permissions and business aims. During days 31–60, select two or three representative workflows and connect their material requirements to practical enforcement and approval rules. During days 61–90, test prohibited actions and recovery, review the real human workload and economics, then record a decision to continue, restrict, repair or stop. These are suggested management milestones, not a statutory timetable.

At the next governance meeting, ask for the action being authorised, the person accountable for its consequence, the limit enforced at runtime, the last failed-action test, the stop authority and the benefit after control costs. If these cannot be demonstrated, the sensible decision is to keep authority narrow until the evidence improves.

Primary evidence and further reading

Sources checked 7 November 2026: EU AI Act amending regulation (EU) 2026/1744; European Commission AI Act overview; ISO/IEC 42001, ISO/IEC 27090 and ISO/IEC 42007 draft; NIST AI RMF; Singapore IMDA agentic governance guidance; OWASP GenAI Security Project; MITRE ATLAS; and CSA AI Controls Matrix. This briefing is executive management guidance, not legal advice or evidence of compliance for a particular system.
